Updated on:  October 13, 2026 / 9:14 PM EDT
            / CBS News

Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Wednesday, Oct. 14, here. See earlier developments below.

Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell on residential areas in Riyadh on Tuesday, injuring four people and damaging 15 homes.

State-run Saudi Press Agency reported the injured included two women, a man and a child. Images released by Saudi's Civil Defense showed broken windows caused by what it said was fallen shrapnel.

The Saudi Ministry of Energy said a limited fire broke out in an administrative building in Aramco, one of the world's largest oil facilities, that was targeted in the country's Eastern Province. The ministry said no injuries were reported.

The attack comes as the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi coalition exchanged attacks Tuesday night. It marks a fresh escalation in the widening Middle East crisis and came shortly after the Saudi coalition reported a series of alerts for incoming missiles heading for the country's Eastern Province, a major oil-producing region and the capital Riyadh.

Amid Houthi attacks across Saudi Arabia, the U.S. Department of State announced Tuesday it is requiring government employees to have special authorization from a chief of mission to use any airport in the kingdom.

U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia are also not allowed to travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border due to safety risks and need special authorization for travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu and Taif, according to the State Department's security alert.

"U.S. citizens should be aware of potential attacks on airports, flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions," the alert reads. "Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia. We recommend checking your flight departure status directly with the airline and with the airport."

Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authorities have suspended operations at the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh through Oct. 17. King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam are still operational with delays and cancellations, according to the State Department.

The Saudi-led coalition battling the Iran-backed Houthis confirmed it struck oil sites across western Yemen on Tuesday, including in the capital Sanaa, in response to the deadliest attack on the kingdom's soil in years.

Blasts were heard shortly after in Saudi capital Riyadh and at an oil giant Aramco facility in eastern Saudi Arabia, witnesses and journalists told AFP.

Tuesday's coalition strikes in Yemen's Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to "supply the war effort" by the Houthis to "threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways," coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X.

An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said earlier that "Saudi aggression" targeted the oil firm.

A tanker and a container ship were hit by projectiles of unknown origin in the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime agency said on Tuesday, as Iran keeps up its blockade of the strategic waterway in place since the start of the Middle East war.

An investigation is underway, United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said, without specifying whether the attacks caused any damage or casualties.

Since the beginning of the war, triggered in late February by U.S. and Israeli strikes against Tehran, Iran has claimed control of the strait and regularly targets ships that try to transit it without its permission.

Washington, in response, has imposed its own naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two Houthi ballistic missiles fired at the kingdom's east, after witnesses heard the sounds of blasts at an Aramco facility in Dhahran.

The coalition announced the "interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia at Dhahran," adding that debris fell in a residential area in the city, which hosts the headquarters of oil giant Aramco.

In a separate statement, the coalition said it intercepted a second missile targeting the city of Harad, also in the Eastern Province.

About 40 minutes later, the spokesperson for the military coalition said they intercepted and destroyed two drones in the Riyadh region and the southern region. It also destroyed three cruise missiles in the same areas.

Iran appears to be targeting commercial vessels conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers in and near the Strait of Hormuz in order to try to undermine vessels' ability to move energy through the strait, the Institute for the Study of War said Tuesday.

Iran may be developing its anti-ship missile capabilities, the U.S.-based think tank said in a post on X.

The U.K.'s Maritime Trade Operations Centre posted on X Monday that at least three vessels had been attacked by unknown projectiles in the strait a day earlier. There were no immediate claims of responsibility.

But Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's top security body, told state TV on Saturday that Iranian forces were striking an average of five "smuggling ships" every night.

Rezaei appeared to be referring to U.S. efforts to guide oil shipments through the strait before the oil is transferred to larger tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke over the phone with Turkey's president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, as the Iran-backed Houthis step up attacks on Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi Foreign Ministry said Erdoğan conveyed condolences for the strikes on Saudi civilian targets, including the airport attack in Riyadh that killed 13 people over the weekend.

"President Erdoğan also affirmed Türkiye's full solidarity with the Kingdom and its support of all measures aimed at safeguarding Saudi Arabia's security and strengthening its stability," the foreign ministry said in a statement.

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a joint defense agreement in August that states an attack on one country should be considered an attack on all of the countries and responded to accordingly.

President Trump was also asked while leaving the White House on Tuesday whether he will urge Erdoğan to help in Saudi Arabia.

"I might do it. He's a great friend of mine, as you know," Mr. Trump told reporters. "And I might do that. I have a lot of respect for the president of Turkey. President Erdoğan, I think, would do as I ask."

Iran has made a "major shift" in its efforts to attack the United Kingdom, including going after harder targets such as military bases, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5 warned Tuesday.

In his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London, Sir Ken McCallum outlined the growing challenges facing the country, from hostile foreign governments and terrorism to the potential misuse of AI. Iran, he said, has demonstrated that it is "keen on subcontracting its U.K. violence … using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites."

"Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities, with whom I want to express solidarity," he said.

"The other major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites," he added.

All of these alleged activities led to more than 50 Iran-linked arrests in the U.K. over the past year alone, McCallum said.

Suspected cholera cases in Yemen have tripled in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating an increasing number of war casualties.

The country's escalating war, combined with mass displacement, is helping infectious disease outbreaks spread, the WHO said, with overcrowding, inadequate access to safe water and disrupted health services exposing more people to cholera, measles and other preventable diseases.

Suspected cholera cases tripled from 217 in the week beginning Sept. 6, to 647 in the week beginning Sept. 27, the U.N. health agency said.

It said Yemeni authorities have reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 cholera deaths this year – with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks alone.

"Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated," said Annette Heinzelmann, the WHO's emergency director for the region. "Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities."

The United Kingdom is advising against all but essential travel to large areas of Saudi Arabia, including the capital city of Riyadh, in the wake of Houthi strikes.

The new warning, released Tuesday, also included several areas the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office warned should be avoided entirely. The area to be avoided entirely is within about 6 miles of the Yemeni border with Saudi Arabia, according to the U.K. Nonessential travel is not advised to Aseer, Riyadh, Najran and Jizan provinces.
